examples: This passage is open to authorized personnel only.
Today only, 20% off everything.
Admission is free for students only.
The counseling is free of charge for the first session only.
Applications are accepted only from residents of this country.
On weekdays only
fields.explain:
Public style: signs, flyers, regulations, event announcements.
Not used with verbs/descriptions of free actions; mainly attaches to nouns indicating a target/time frame.
Usually placed near the beginning of the sentence to set the condition of a special offer/limitation.

• Specifies a special scope of application: "only … can …".
• Tone of announcements, regulations, temporary or permanent offers.
• Often used with words indicating time/target: 本日／女性／会員／学生／初回 など.
• Does not express "the best" like ～に限る, and is different from ～に限って.
fields.notes:
• In policy documents: "Aに限り、Bとする" is the standard regulatory formula.
• The predicate can be omitted on signs: "関係者に限り"。
• Combine with "一部店舗に限り" to state an exception in the area of application.
mistakes: Using it with a verb: "行くに限り" is incorrect; it must attach to a noun.
Confusing it with ～に限る (evaluation "the best"): a different communicative purpose.
Adding は after に限り to make "に限りは" (unnatural); if you need emphasis, use "Nに限っては".
The JLPT often sets traps with the contrasting pair に限り／に限らず; pay attention to the opposite meanings.

fields.connection: V plain form + ばかりでなく… (も) / N / Na + な / Aい + い
examples: Not only can I not ski, but it is also affecting my daily life.
Because of this heat, not only people but animals too have stopped moving and are lying still.
She can speak not only English but also French and German.
This book is not just interesting; it is also useful for work.
"Don't think only about yourself; think about other people's feelings too."
That supermarket not only has a wide range of products, but its prices are also low.
fields.explain: ◎ A way of emphasizing something by mentioning not just one thing but several.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～だけでなく／～はもちろん.
→ ～ばかりでなく means "not only… but also…", is often used in written language, and has a slightly formal nuance.
2) The second clause is usually the point you want to emphasize more.
→ Common structure: AばかりでなくBも／まで.
3) Not used when merely giving examples.
→ For giving examples, use ～など…
meaning_vi: 「～だけでなくて、その他にも…。」
Not only ~, but in addition to that also…
examples: 1. 日本人ばかりでなく、世界中の人がエネルギー問題に関心を持っている。
日本人ばかりでなく、世界中の人がエネルギー問題に関心を持っている。=> Not only Japanese people but people all over the world are interested in energy problems.
2. この番組は、面白いばかりでなく、さまざまなことが学べる。
この番組は、面白いばかりでなく、さまざまなことが学べる。=> This program is not only interesting; you can also learn many different things from it.
3. 彼は町を案内してくれたばかりでなく、この地方の料理もご馳走しててくれた。
彼は町を案内してくれたばかりでなく、この地方の料理もご馳走しててくれた。=> He not only showed me around the town but also treated me to the local cuisine.
meaning_vi: Used when you want to say "not only ~ but also ~"
［ふつう］　+　だけでなく／だけじゃなく（て）／ばかりでなく／ばかりじゃなく（て）
［Na：元気な　N：学生だ］
examples: 1. ➀　部屋だけでなく
Not only the room
2. ②　飛行機だけでなく船にも乗った。
I rode not only a plane but also a ship.
3. ③　この製品は、日本ばかりでなく、海外でも使われている。
This product is used not only in Japan but also overseas.
4. ➃　今日は、風が強いばかりでなく、雨も降るらしい。
I hear that today it will not only be windy but also rain.
5. ⑤　考えるだけじゃなくて、実際にやってみなくちゃ。
Don't just think about it; you have to actually try it.

examples: I should have apologized then.
I should have gone to the doctor sooner.
I wish I hadn't bought an expensive camera.
If I had known it would rain, I would have brought an umbrella.
You should have told him the truth.
I should have asked
fields.explain:
A strong nuance of regret or self-blame.
It can be used in a gentle tone, sometimes conveying self-reproach or wistfulness.
A softer form can add: ～ばよかったのに → "If only…, yet…" (with a slight complaint or reproach).

•
Expresses regret about something in the past that you did not do (or did).

•
Natural translations: "If only…", "I should have…", "I wish I had…".

• Usually refers to an action that was not done but should have been, or an action that was done but you wish you hadn't.
• This is an emotional expression, used a lot in conversation, movies, and inner monologues in diaries.
fields.notes:
• This is an N3–N2 grammar point that appears often in conversation and in the listening and reading sections of exams.
• In casual speech, だ can be omitted: ～ばよかったなぁ, ～ばよかったのに….
• It can be followed by って → ～ばよかったって for emphasis when reporting.
meaning_vi: If only … it would have been good
explain: Used to express regret about something that happened differently from what you wanted
examples: 1. 遅刻してしまった。もっと早く家を出ればよかった。
I was late. I should have left home earlier.
2. 田中さんにあんなことを言わなければよかった。
I wish I hadn't said such things to Tanaka.
meaning_vi: And yet…/ If only…
explain: Used to express regret about something that happened differently from what you wanted
examples: 1. パーテイー、楽しかったよ。君も行けばよかったのに。
The party was fun. You should have come too.
2. 安かったら買うのに。
If it were cheap, I would buy it, but…
mistakes: Using the wrong verb tense: you must use Vば or Vたら.
Confusing it with ～といい／～ばいい (a wish about the future).
Dropping よかった and using only Vば → wrong meaning.
For the negative, you must use なければよかった or なかったらよかった.

rows: Regret about an action not taken.
Very close in meaning, with a softer or neutral nuance.
Adds a clearer nuance of complaint and regret.
<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってくれれ ばよかったのに。
It would be good if… (future wish)
Used for future wishes, not regret about the past.
<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>える といいね。

examples: With speeches, the more you practice, the better you get.
The higher the salary, the happier I am.
With foreign languages, anyone gets better the more they practice.
The more I think about the future, the more anxious I become.
The more I look at it, the more wonderful this painting is.
The bigger your dream, the better.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes a proportional relationship: increase–increase or decrease–decrease (少なければ少ないほど…).
The second clause can deny absoluteness with ～とは限らない／～わけではない.
With Aな/N, the form であればあるほど is formal/precise in written language.
In conversation, the first clause can be shortened if the context is clear:若ければ若いほど…

- Meaning: "The more A, the more B". Expresses a covariant relationship or an increase/decrease in one direction.
- Form: The same word class is repeated in the two halves before ～ば and ～ほど to create a comparison of degree.
- Scope: Used for general tendencies/relationships; rarely used for a single, one-time event.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～ばいい (simple condition).
→ ～ば～ほど expresses a parallel increase/decrease: "the more… the more…".
2) The two clauses change in the same direction.
→ If there is no sense of "degree increasing accordingly", this pattern does not fit.
3) Pay attention to the conjugation.
→ V/A in the ba-form in the first clause; the second clause usually comes with ほど (can be omitted in some sentences). explain: Used to show that the degree of the result increases as the characteristic of the thing increases ⏐ examples: 1. 彼のことを知れば知るほど好きになる。
The more I get to know him, the more I like him.
2. 荷物は少なければ少ないほどいい。
The less luggage, the better. | Na form: Naなら Naなほど
mistakes: Wrong repeated form: using different forms in the two clauses (× 行けば行ったほど) → it must be Vば・Vる.
Using it for a single event rather than a tendency → unnatural.
Incorrect with Aな/N: forgetting な/である before ほど (× 静かほど) → 静かなほど／静かであるほど.
Confusing it with "～ほど～はない" (superlative) → a completely different meaning.

rows: Emphasizes change over time/a process; no need to repeat the word
<ruby>温度<rt>おんど</rt></ruby>が<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がるにつれて<ruby>氷<rt>こおり</rt></ruby>が<ruby>溶<rt>と</rt></ruby>ける。
Unlike the proportional "the more… the more…" model, it only indicates degree
<ruby>驚<rt>おどろ</rt></ruby>くほど<ruby>美<rt>うつく</rt></ruby>しい。
～と also expresses a regular relationship, but ～ば～ほど emphasizes degree
<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べると<ruby>元気<rt>げんき</rt></ruby>になる。

fields.connection: V plain form + ふりをする / N + の / Na + な / Aい
examples: He pretended not to notice the question.
The child pretended to be asleep and waited for the sweets.
She is pretending to be fine, but actually she is having a hard time.
He is pretending to be an adult and trying to look more grown-up than he is.
I pretended it didn't hurt, but it hurt quite a lot.
fields.explain:
Used to describe behavior that hides the truth; often carries an implied evaluation (insincere/evasive).
Often combined with して/している to state a purpose or a continuing state.
Not used for natural phenomena/inanimate things (×雨が降らないふりをする).

• Expresses pretending, acting as if in some state/behavior while the reality is different.
• The subject is usually a conscious person/animal; it has a nuance of insincerity, sometimes with a critical meaning.
• Both past and present tense can be used: 知らないふりをした (pretended), している (is pretending).
fields.notes:
• Negative: ～ふりをしない (not put on an act). Past: ～ふりをした.
• An evaluative adjective can be inserted: わざと～、いかにも～のふり。
• In conversation, add 「なんて」 for criticism: 知らないふりなんてやめて。
mistakes: Wrong particle with nouns: it must be Nのふりをする, not Nなふりをする.
Using it with an inanimate subject is incorrect: × ドアが壊れたふりをする.
Confusing it with ～かのようだ: that pattern describes outward appearance, not "pretending".
Forgetting to keep 「な」 with na-adjectives: × 元気ふりをする → ◯ 元気なふりをする.

<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らぬ<ruby>体<rt>からだ</rt></ruby>／<ruby>悲<rt>かな</rt></ruby>しげ

examples: If you have an income, you should pay taxes as a citizen.
The professor told me to read as many as 30 books.
I should have studied harder when I was a student.
You should not say things that hurt people. (=～してはならない)
*Knock before entering the room.
She has a lovable personality, and is liked by everyone.
fields.explain:
More formal than ～たほうがいい, conveying responsibility or moral principle.
It can sound somewhat imposing if used in the wrong context, since it expresses a strong opinion.
It is very suitable in written language, speeches, and social judgments.
When talking about your own actions → softer, expressing self-reproach.

•
Expresses what should be done or must be done based on morality, common sense, or responsibility.

• Has a nuance of the speaker's subjective judgment but with a universal character: "everyone should do this".
• Can be used to criticize, advise, or emphasize moral obligation.
• Natural translations: "should…", "must…", "ought to have…".
fields.notes:
• Polite negative form → ～べきではありません.
• In casual speech, a softer form can be used: ～べきだったなぁ (I should have…).
• Old-fashioned form used a lot in law and official documents: ～すべし (must…).
mistakes: Using ～べきだ with older people/superiors may be seen as impolite.
Confusing it with ～たほうがいい – use べきだ when the opinion is about "right/wrong, should/must", not general advice.
Dropping だ at the end when writing the standard formal form is incorrect (it must have だ or です).
The JLPT often tests the distinction from ～はずだ and ～なければならない.

rows: <ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>らなければならない。

examples: You should not break a promise.
You should not share other people's personal information.
You should not make decisions based on your emotions.
You shouldn't walk alone on a road like this at night.
I should not have made such a careless remark.
fields.explain:
Used for general standards: morality, professional rules, safety, manners.
In casual communication, it can be softened: ～ないほうがいい／やめたほうがいい.
Not used for simple ability/permission; that is the scope of ～てはいけない／～てもいい.

• Expresses "should not/ought not" based on social rules, morality, common sense, professional standards.
• Stronger than "ないほうがいい" (advice), weaker than "てはいけない" (legal/regulatory prohibition).
• Usually an objective judgment; use it according to context to avoid being too imposing.
fields.notes:
• "するべきではない" is used in practice, but in proper writing: "すべきではない".
• A passive/vague-topic structure helps make it objective: 個人を特定する発言はすべきではない。
• When speaking within an organization, add grounds to make it less imposing: 安全面から見て、～すべきではない。
mistakes: Using it instead of "てはいけない" on signs/strict regulations → the nuance does not fit.
Confusing it with "ことはない": the latter means "there is no need", not "should not".
The JLPT often asks for the conversion: するべきではない ⇄ すべきではない.
Outdated/unnatural: × 行くべきではないと思いますか → better: 行かないほうがいいと思います (when it is just light personal advice).

rows: <ruby>嘘<rt>うそ</rt></ruby>をつくべきではない。
<ruby>夜<rt>よる</rt></ruby><ruby>更<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>かしはないほうがいい。
ここで<ruby>喫煙<rt>きつえん</rt></ruby>してはいけない。
Expresses that something is unnecessary, not prohibition/should not
<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>することはない。

fields.meaning: To the extent that, the more… the more…
fields.connection: V plain form・Aい・N + ほど / Vば Vる + ほど
examples: This paper is so difficult that it makes me want to stop reading halfway through.
I worked all day, so I'm so tired that I can't walk anymore.
There was a hole about the size of a 100-yen coin in my pants.
I'm sorry, please wait about 10 minutes.
I can get from home to school in about 30 minutes.
I was so troubled that I couldn't even sleep at night.
fields.explain:
Used to emphasize degree or a strong comparison.
Can be used with both positive and negative emotions.
In casual speech, people use 「～くらい」 instead of 「～ほど」.
Formal nuance, common in written language, essays, and JLPT exams.

•
① Degree "to the extent that…": Expresses a high degree of a state/action.

•
② Comparison: "Nothing is as…, no one is as…": Often used in the structure「Aほど～はない」＝ "There is nothing as … as A".

•
③ The more… the more…: Shows a directly proportional relationship between the two clauses.

•
Note: Mostly written language / JLPT; it can be used in spoken language but less often.
fields.notes:
1) ～ほど is easily confused with ～くらい.
→ The meaning "about/approximately" is similar, but ～ほど is usually more formal and often used in written language.
2) Be careful because ～ほど has many uses (degree, extreme…).
→ In the same test, ～ほど may appear with different meanings (to the extent that, ~ is the best), making it easy to fall into a trap when choosing the answer.
3) Look at the accompanying structure to determine the meaning.
→ If it indicates a quantity/estimate: the meaning is "about".
→ If it is used with a comparison/extreme: it probably has a different meaning.
mistakes: Using it incorrectly when there is no correlation → you need the logic: however much A changes → B changes that much.
Confusing it with くらい: くらい is more casual and not used in formal writing.
The form "VればVるほど" requires the verb to be repeated.
Often appears in JLPT N3-N2 in the forms "AほどBはない", "Vるほど".

rows: To the extent…, the more…, nothing is as…
More formal; used in strong comparisons or for degree.
<ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>く ほど<ruby>嬉<rt>うれ</rt></ruby>しかった。
Spoken language, lighter than ほど.
<ruby>死<rt>し</rt></ruby>ぬ くらい<ruby>疲<rt>つか</rt></ruby>れた。
Expresses the correlation between two actions/states.
<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>れば<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>る ほど<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きになる。
<ruby>彼女<rt>かのじょ</rt></ruby>ほど<ruby>優<rt>やさ</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>はいない。

examples: The air was stuffy, so I left the window open for a while.
I'll tidy up later, so please leave it as it is.
Leave the power switched off
I've kept this potted plant outside the whole summer.
Please leave it as it is.
fields.explain: ◎ Continuing the same state as it is now.

examples: It's a rare opportunity, so please do take part.
He rarely fails.
Conditions this good are really rare.
Crimes rarely happen in this town.
This is a rare name.
A heat wave like this year's is rare.
fields.explain:
Used to present rarity as a property of N, not focusing on a repeated action.
In formal language, it can be replaced by まれな／きわめてまれな (very rare).
Polite: ～はめったにありません. Past: ～はめったになかった.

• Expresses that a "thing/event" is rare and hardly ever exists/happens. It is an evaluation of the rarity of the target.
• Unlike めったに～ない (540), which emphasizes "frequency of an action", this pattern emphasizes "the rarity of the opportunity/event itself".
• Often used with nouns such as 機会, チャンス, 例, こと, ケース, 出来事, 名前, 品物.
fields.notes:
• An emphatic structure can be used: こんなことは本当にめったにない.
• In terms of nuance, めったにない often conveys a "precious opportunity": 今回はめったにないチャンスだ.
• Avoid using "めったにある": it is unnatural; use the negative "めったにない".
mistakes: Confusing it with めったに～ない: めったにない must go with a noun or a nominalized clause.
Misunderstanding "ない" as negating the whole sentence: めったにない has the affirmative meaning "rare", not "not".
JLPT: choose correctly between "めったにない機会" and "めったに行かない" according to the required structure.
Wrong tense: × めったにないでした → ✓ めったにありませんでした / めったになかった.

rows: Modifies N or evaluates an event
めったにない<ruby>機会<rt>きかい</rt></ruby>
まれな／<ruby>希少<rt>きしょう</rt></ruby>な

examples: A shop like that? I'll never go there again!
There's no way he'd be late. He's a very serious person.
This is anything but easy. It'll take at least a week.
I won't be fooled again!
There's no way she would lie.
Believe a rumor like that? Never.
fields.explain:
Usually used in spoken language with strong emotion; be careful about politeness when speaking to a superior.
Uses an affirmative form to emphasize negation (rhetorical question): "〜ものか" is equivalent to "No way ~".
In conversation, the subject and the preceding part can be omitted, blurting out just "〜ものか".

• Strong, emotional negation: "No way/Never/Not in a million years…".
• Used to reject the other person's invitation, evaluation, or assertion; can also be said to oneself.
• Sounds harsh if said directly; 〜もんですか/〜ものですか is slightly softer but still strong.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～わけがない.
→ ～ものか is a strong negation expressing emotional volition/opposition (no way, definitely not).
2) Usually used in spoken language.
→ Often has a nuance of anger, determination, or rebuttal.
3) Not used for mild negation.
→ For "not exactly" or soft negation, use a different pattern.
mistakes: Incorrect combination with na-adjectives: × 静かなものか → ✓ 静かなものか.
Using it in formal written language → does not fit the style; choose わけがない/はずがない.
Confusing it with a real question: "〜ものか" is a strong negation, not a question asking for information.
